planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Black Beauty is a Geranium pratense hybrid selected primarily for its near-black summer foliage rather than flower power.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Black Beauty is grown chiefly for its deeply divided, near-black to dark chocolate-bronze foliage, a striking foil for silver or chartreuse companions through most of the growing season, with small lavender-blue flowers appearing as a secondary feature in early summer. Foliage color deepens in strong sun and can fade toward green in heavy shade, so give it an open, sunny spot for the darkest leaf effect. Cut back hard after flowering to refresh the foliage mound for the remainder of the season, and divide congested clumps in spring every few years.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; a bronze-foliage hybrid geranium related to 'Black Beauty' but selected for pink rather than blue flowers.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. This compact hybrid pairs deeply cut, dark bronze-chocolate foliage with soft pink flowers through early summer, giving a gentler color contrast than the blue-flowered 'Black Beauty' it is related to. The low, mounding habit suits the front of a border or a container where the foliage color can be appreciated up close all season. Shear lightly after the main flush of bloom to tidy the mound and encourage some repeat flowering, and keep soil from staying soggy over winter.

common_name: Bill Wallis Pyrenean Cranesbill (Deep Purple Dwarf Geranium)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; this selection of Pyrenean cranesbill self-sows readily, so established plantings persist and spread through volunteer seedlings.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Bill Wallis is a dwarf, airy selection of the Pyrenean cranesbill, bearing a long summer succession of small but intensely saturated violet-purple flowers over finely cut, low foliage. It seeds itself gently into gravel paths, wall crevices, and border edges, behaving more like a long-lived cottage-garden annual than a typical clump-forming perennial, and surplus seedlings are easily hoed out or transplanted. Little maintenance is needed beyond removing unwanted seedlings and dividing congested crowns occasionally in spring.

common_name: Amy Doncaster Wood Cranesbill (Violet-Blue White-Eyed Geranium)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; a classic named selection of wood cranesbill valued for unusually deep flower color with a contrasting white eye.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun. Amy Doncaster produces an early-summer flush of rich violet-blue flowers, each marked at the center with a small, crisp white eye that gives the display more depth than the plain-colored species. It forms an upright clump of deeply lobed foliage that associates well with early perennials and spring-flowering shrubs in a lightly shaded border. Cut the foliage back hard after flowering to keep the clump tidy through summer, and divide every three to four years to maintain vigor.

common_name: Bressingham Flair Armenian Cranesbill (Compact Magenta-Eyed Geranium)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; a more compact selection of Armenian cranesbill bred for smaller gardens.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Bressingham Flair carries the same vivid magenta-pink flowers with a near-black central eye and dark veining as the species Armenian cranesbill, but on a noticeably more compact, restrained plant better suited to smaller borders. Established clumps bloom heavily for several weeks in early summer, and the lax stems benefit from discreet staking or the support of sturdier neighbors to keep the display upright. Shear back after flowering to tidy the foliage and divide every few years as the center of the clump thins.

common_name: Springtime Mourning Widow Cranesbill (Cream-Splashed Spring Foliage Geranium)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil in partial to full shade; grown as much for its cream-marked emerging foliage as for its dusky flowers.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil in partial to full shade. Springtime opens its season with young leaves heavily splashed and mottled in cream and pale yellow, an effect that fades toward plain green as the foliage matures through early summer, after which the plant produces the dusky maroon-purple nodding flowers typical of mourning widow geranium. The variegation is most pronounced in cool spring weather and in sites with reliable moisture, so avoid dry shade where the cream markings fade quickly. Remove flowering stems after bloom to keep the clump neat, and divide in spring if the variegated effect begins to weaken.

common_name: Southcombe Star Cranesbill (Starry Striped Pink Hybrid Geranium)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; one of several named oxonianum selections raised in Devon, England.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Southcombe Star bears narrow, star-shaped pale pink petals finely pencilled with darker veining, giving a lighter, more delicate look than the solid-colored 'Wargrave Pink' or 'Claridge Druce'. It shares the vigorous, mildew-resistant constitution typical of x oxonianum hybrids, forming a wide mound of semi-evergreen foliage that blooms over a long season from late spring into autumn. Shear back hard after the first flush to renew foliage and prompt further flowering, and divide every few years to keep the clump vigorous.

common_name: Nunwood Purple Bloody Cranesbill (Deep Purple Dwarf Geranium)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun; a compact bloody cranesbill selection valued for unusually deep purple flower color.

directions: Plant in average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun. Nunwood Purple forms a low, dense mound of finely cut foliage covered through early summer in flowers of a notably deeper reddish-purple than the species or than paler cultivars such as 'Elke', fading to attractive orange and red tones in fall. Like other bloody cranesbill selections it tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil once established, making it a durable choice for rock gardens, path edges, and sunny slopes. Shear lightly after the main bloom flush to tidy the mound, and divide only occasionally, as the species resents frequent disturbance.

common_name: Becky Towe Garden Phlox (Variegated Foliage Orange-Eyed Phlox)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in fertile, moisture-retentive, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; good air circulation reduces powdery mildew on the variegated foliage.

directions: Plant in fertile, moisture-retentive, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Becky Towe pairs leaves edged and streaked in creamy yellow with clusters of salmon-pink flowers centered on a vivid orange-red eye, giving it a two-season appeal that plain-leaved garden phlox cultivars lack. The variegation holds best with consistent moisture and some afternoon shade in hot climates, while full sun with good airflow keeps the foliage cleanest. Deadhead spent flower trusses to prolong bloom and thin stems in spring to improve air circulation and reduce powdery mildew.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in fertile, moisture-retentive, well-drained soil in full sun; a long-cultivated Dutch garden phlox valued for its sturdy stems and reliable performance.

directions: Plant in fertile, moisture-retentive, well-drained soil in full sun. Rijnstroom produces large, rounded flower trusses in a deep rose-purple over sturdy, upright stems that rarely need staking, flowering reliably from midsummer onward. It has remained a popular choice in European perennial borders for decades thanks to its dependable vigor and good resistance to flopping in wind and rain compared with many older garden phlox cultivars. Thin stems in spring to improve air circulation and reduce powdery mildew, and divide congested clumps every three to four years to maintain bloom quality.

common_name: White Admiral Garden Phlox (Classic Pure White Phlox)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in fertile, moisture-retentive, well-drained soil in full sun; an old, widely grown white garden phlox valued for its clean color and dependable vigor.

directions: Plant in fertile, moisture-retentive, well-drained soil in full sun. White Admiral bears large, rounded trusses of pure white flowers on tall, sturdy stems from midsummer into early fall, brightening the back of a border or working as a cut flower. Its vigorous, long-lived clumps have kept it in cultivation for decades as a dependable standard among white-flowered garden phlox selections. Thin stems to roughly five or six per clump in spring to improve air circulation and reduce powdery mildew, and divide every three to four years to maintain vigor.

common_name: Europa Garden Phlox (White with Red-Pink Eye)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in fertile, moisture-retentive, well-drained soil in full sun; a long-established bicolor garden phlox prized for its crisp contrast between white petals and a carmine-red eye.

directions: Plant in fertile, moisture-retentive, well-drained soil in full sun. Europa opens white flowers each stamped with a distinct carmine-red eye, a crisp bicolor combination that reads clearly from a distance and has kept this long-established cultivar popular in traditional perennial borders. Large, rounded trusses appear on sturdy stems from midsummer onward, and the plant holds its color well without fading in heat. Thin stems in spring to improve airflow and reduce powdery mildew, and divide every three to four years as clumps become congested.

common_name: Minnie Pearl Garden Phlox (Early-Blooming Compact White Phlox)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in fertile, moisture-retentive, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; blooms earlier than most tall garden phlox cultivars.

directions: Plant in fertile, moisture-retentive, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Minnie Pearl produces slender trusses of pure white flowers in early summer, ahead of most garden phlox cultivars, on a compact plant with notably good resistance to powdery mildew compared with many older white-flowered selections. Its smaller stature and early timing make it useful for bridging the gap between spring perennials and the main midsummer phlox display. Deadhead to tidy the plant after bloom and divide every few years to keep clumps vigorous.

common_name: Maischnee Moss Phlox (Compact White Creeping Phlox)

planting.note: Plant in well-drained to dry, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; a German-raised white moss phlox selection valued for a tight, compact habit.

directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Maischnee, German for 'May snow,' covers its needle-like evergreen foliage in a dense flush of pure white flowers each spring, on a noticeably tighter and more compact mat than looser-growing white selections such as 'Snowflake'. The dense habit makes it useful for small rock garden pockets, trough plantings, and the edges of stone paths where a sprawling cultivar would quickly overrun its neighbors. Shear lightly after bloom to keep the mat tight and encourage dense regrowth, and keep the site sharply drained to avoid crown rot.

common_name: G.F. Wilson Moss Phlox (Classic Lavender-Blue Creeping Phlox)

planting.note: Plant in well-drained to dry, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; one of the oldest named moss phlox selections still offered, grown for its soft lavender-blue flower color.

directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. G.F. Wilson is a historic moss phlox selection that blankets its needle-like evergreen foliage each spring in soft lavender-blue flowers, a muted, cooler tone distinct from the brighter blue-violet of 'Emerald Blue'. Long in cultivation, it forms a dense, fast-spreading evergreen mat well suited to rock gardens, slopes, and wall plantings. Shear lightly after flowering to keep the mat compact and dense, and avoid rich or poorly drained soil, which encourages floppy growth and crown rot.
